rows.stem: The ratio of the magnitudes of the electric field and magnetic field of a plane electromagnetic wave is
rows.solution:
**The answer is (C): the ratio is \(c\).**

**The relation.** For a plane electromagnetic wave travelling in vacuum, Maxwell's equations force the two field amplitudes into a fixed ratio:

\(\dfrac{E_0}{B_0} = \dfrac{E}{B} = c = 3 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)

The same ratio holds at every instant, not merely between the peaks, because the two fields oscillate **in phase** — they reach their maxima together and cross zero together.

**Where it comes from.** A changing magnetic field induces an electric field (Faraday) and a changing electric field induces a magnetic one (Ampère-Maxwell). Requiring the two induced fields to sustain each other as a travelling wave fixes both the speed and the amplitude ratio, and gives

\(c = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}}\)

**Reading the ratio correctly.** Since \(c\) is large, \(E_0\) is numerically some \(10^{8}\) times \(B_0\) in SI units — a wave with \(E_0 = 30\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}\) has \(B_0 = 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{T}\). That makes the magnetic field *look* negligible, and it is not. The two carry **exactly equal energy**:

\(u_E = \dfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0E_0^{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{B_0^{2}}{\mu_0} = u_B\)

The factor \(1/\mu_0\) in the magnetic energy density restores the balance that \(E_0 = cB_0\) appears to destroy. The disparity is an artefact of the SI units, not of the physics.

Note also that this is a ratio with **dimensions** — it is a speed, not a pure number — which alone rules out the option "1".

rows.subtopic: Line Spectra of the Hydrogen Atom
rows.stem: Specify the transition of electron in the wavelength of the line in the Bohr model of hydrogen atom which gives rise to the spectral line of highest wavelength.
rows.solution:
**The answer is (B): \(n = 3\) to \(n = 2\).**

**The principle.** The photon's wavelength and its energy are inversely related:

\(\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{\Delta E}\)

So the **highest** wavelength comes from the **smallest** energy drop. The question is therefore not which transition is biggest but which is **smallest**.

**Comparing the four**, using \(E_n = -\dfrac{13{\cdot}6}{n^{2}}\ \mathrm{eV}\):

| Transition | \(\Delta E\) | \(\lambda\) |
|---|---|---|
| \(3 \to 1\) | \(13{\cdot}6\left(1 - \tfrac{1}{9}\right) = 12{\cdot}09\) eV | \(1026\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}}\) |
| \(4 \to 1\) | \(13{\cdot}6\left(1 - \tfrac{1}{16}\right) = 12{\cdot}75\) eV | \(973\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}}\) |
| \(4 \to 2\) | \(13{\cdot}6\left(\tfrac{1}{4} - \tfrac{1}{16}\right) = 2{\cdot}55\) eV | \(4862\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}}\) |
| **\(3 \to 2\)** | \(13{\cdot}6\left(\tfrac{1}{4} - \tfrac{1}{9}\right) = \mathbf{1{\cdot}89}\) **eV** | \(\mathbf{6563\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}}}\) |

\(3 \to 2\) is the smallest drop and therefore the longest wavelength.

**A shortcut that avoids all four calculations.** Levels crowd together as \(n\) rises, so a transition between two **high, adjacent** levels releases the least energy. Of the four offered, \(3 \to 2\) is the only one that is both adjacent and does not reach down to the ground state — and every transition ending on \(n = 1\) is enormous by comparison, because \(n = 1\) lies \(10{\cdot}2\) eV below \(n = 2\).

**What this line is.** \(6563\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}}\) is \(H_\alpha\), the first line of the **Balmer** series and the brightest visible hydrogen line — the deep red that colours hydrogen discharge tubes and emission nebulae. The two transitions ending on \(n = 1\) belong to the ultraviolet Lyman series and are invisible.

rows.stem: An isolated point charge particle produces an electric field \(\vec{\mathrm{E}}\) at a point 3 m away from it. The distance of the point at which the field is \(\dfrac{\vec{\mathrm{E}}}{4}\) will be
rows.solution:
**The answer is (D): 6 m.**

**The law.** The field of an isolated point charge falls off as the inverse square of the distance:

\(E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r^{2}} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad E \propto \dfrac{1}{r^{2}}\)

**Applying it.** Taking the ratio of the two points removes \(q\) and all the constants:

\(\dfrac{E_2}{E_1} = \left(\dfrac{r_1}{r_2}\right)^{2}\)

We want \(E_2 = \dfrac{E_1}{4}\), so

\(\dfrac{1}{4} = \left(\dfrac{3}{r_2}\right)^{2} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{3}{r_2}\)

\(r_2 = 6\ \mathrm{m}\)

**The trap is the square root.** Quartering the field requires only a **doubling** of the distance, not a quadrupling — yet "4 m" sits in the option list to catch the reader who subtracts or adds rather than scales, and "2 m" catches the one who moves in the wrong direction entirely. The rule to carry: with an inverse-square law, dividing the field by \(n^{2}\) means multiplying the distance by \(n\).

**A caution about the wording.** The stem calls \(\vec{\mathrm{E}}\) a vector and then asks about \(\vec{\mathrm{E}}/4\). Since the field of a point charge is radial, the direction is the same at both points and only the magnitude is in question — so the vector notation adds nothing here beyond a reminder that the two points lie on the same radial line.

rows.stem: A steady current of 8 mA flows through a wire. The number of electrons passing through a cross-section of the wire in 10 s is
rows.solution:
**The answer is (B): \(5{\cdot}0 \times 10^{17}\).**

**Charge first, then count.** Current is the rate of flow of charge, so the charge that passes in 10 s is

\(q = It = 8 \times 10^{-3} \times 10 = 8 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{C}\)

That charge is carried by electrons, each of charge \(e = 1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}\) C, so the number of them is

\(n = \dfrac{q}{e} = \dfrac{8 \times 10^{-2}}{1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}}\)

\(n = 5{\cdot}0 \times 10^{17}\)

**Two places the question tries to trip you.** The current is in **milli**amperes, so \(8\ \mathrm{mA} = 8 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{A}\); reading it as 8 A gives \(5 \times 10^{20}\). And the time must be multiplied in — an answer of \(5 \times 10^{16}\) is the count for one second, which is what you get by forgetting \(t\).

**A note on scale.** Half a billion billion electrons cross the wire in ten seconds, and yet 8 mA is a small current — the sort that runs an LED. The reconciliation is that each electron carries an extraordinarily small charge, and that the electrons themselves drift at well under a millimetre per second. A wire carries a large current not because its carriers are fast but because there are so many of them.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.subtopic: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors
rows.stem:
Which one of the following elements will require the highest energy to take out an electron from them ?
Pb, Ge, C and Si
rows.solution:
**The answer is (B): carbon.**

**What the question is asking.** All four elements — lead, germanium, carbon and silicon — are **tetravalent** and sit in the same group of the periodic table. What separates them is the **energy band gap** \(E_g\), the energy an electron must be given to jump from the valence band into the conduction band, which is exactly the "energy to take out an electron" the stem means.

| Element | \(E_g\) | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **Carbon** (diamond) | \(\approx 5{\cdot}5\) eV | **insulator** |
| Silicon | \(\approx 1{\cdot}1\) eV | semiconductor |
| Germanium | \(\approx 0{\cdot}7\) eV | semiconductor |
| Lead | \(\approx 0\) | conductor (metal) |

Carbon requires by far the most, so it is the answer.

**The pattern, and why it runs that way.** Going **down** the group — C, Si, Ge, Sn, Pb — the atoms get larger, the valence electrons sit further from the nucleus and are held more loosely, and the gap **narrows** steadily until it closes altogether at lead, which is a metal. The four elements in this question are simply that sequence read backwards.

**Why the gap decides everything.** Thermal energy at room temperature is only about \(0{\cdot}026\) eV. Against germanium's \(0{\cdot}7\) eV that is small but not hopeless, so a few electrons make the jump and the crystal conducts weakly. Against diamond's \(5{\cdot}5\) eV it is utterly negligible, and the conduction band stays empty — which is why diamond is one of the best electrical insulators known, and also why it is transparent: visible photons carry at most about \(3\) eV, too little to lift an electron across the gap, so they pass straight through instead of being absorbed.

rows.stem: A conductor of 10 \(\Omega\) is connected across a 6 V ideal source. The power supplied by the source to the conductor is
rows.solution:
**The answer is (C): \(3{\cdot}6\) W.**

**The source is ideal**, which is the word that makes this a one-line question: it has no internal resistance, so the full 6 V appears across the conductor and none is lost inside the source.

\(P = \dfrac{V^{2}}{R} = \dfrac{(6)^{2}}{10} = \dfrac{36}{10}\)

\(P = 3{\cdot}6\ \mathrm{W}\)

**Checking it the long way**, which also confirms the route:

\(I = \dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{6}{10} = 0{\cdot}6\ \mathrm{A} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad P = VI = 6 \times 0{\cdot}6 = 3{\cdot}6\ \mathrm{W}\)

and \(P = I^{2}R = (0{\cdot}6)^{2} \times 10 = 3{\cdot}6\) W. All three forms of the power formula agree, as they must.

**Picking the right form matters.** \(P = V^{2}/R\), \(P = I^{2}R\) and \(P = VI\) are equivalent **only** when \(V\) and \(I\) refer to the same element and Ohm's law connects them. Using \(P = I^{2}R\) with the source voltage in place of the current — that is, computing \(6^{2} \times 10\) — is the error the distractors are built around.

**Because the source is ideal, the power it supplies and the power the conductor dissipates are the same number.** Had the source carried an internal resistance \(r\), the two would differ: the source would still supply \(EI\), but \(I^{2}r\) of it would be wasted heating the source itself, and only the remainder would reach the conductor.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation and the Photon
rows.stem: A photon of wavelength 663 nm is incident on a metal surface. The work function of the metal is 1.50 eV. The maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photo electrons is
rows.solution:
**The answer is (B): \(6{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-20}\) J.**

**The photon's energy.**

\(E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^{8}}{663 \times 10^{-9}}\)

\(E = \dfrac{1{\cdot}989 \times 10^{-25}}{6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-7}} = 3{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}\)

The numbers are chosen so that 663 divides 6.63 exactly — worth spotting, since it turns the division into a shift of the exponent.

**The work function, in the same units.**

\(\phi_0 = 1{\cdot}50\ \mathrm{eV} = 1{\cdot}50 \times 1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19} = 2{\cdot}4 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}\)

This conversion is the step the question is really testing: the photon energy comes out in joules and the work function is given in electronvolts, and the two cannot be subtracted until they agree. All four options are in joules, so the answer must be too.

**Einstein's photoelectric equation.**

\(K_{\max} = E - \phi_0 = (3{\cdot}0 - 2{\cdot}4) \times 10^{-19} = 0{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}\)

\(K_{\max} = 6{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-20}\ \mathrm{J}\)

**A check in electronvolts.** \(E = 3{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-19}/1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19} = 1{\cdot}875\) eV, so \(K_{\max} = 1{\cdot}875 - 1{\cdot}50 = 0{\cdot}375\) eV, and \(0{\cdot}375 \times 1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19} = 6{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-20}\) J. The two routes agree.

Note that the photon energy exceeds the work function by only a quarter of an electronvolt, so this red light — 663 nm — is barely above the threshold for this metal, whose threshold wavelength is about \(8280\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}}\), in the near infrared.

rows.subtopic: Refraction and Reflection of Plane Waves
rows.stem: A ray of light of wavelength 600 nm propagates from air into a medium. If its wavelength in the medium becomes 400 nm, the refractive index of the medium is
rows.solution:
**The answer is (B): \(1{\cdot}5\).**

**What survives the boundary and what does not.** When light passes from one medium into another its **frequency is unchanged** — the wave in the second medium is driven by the wave in the first, oscillation for oscillation, so the two must keep time. What changes is the **speed**, and with it the wavelength, since \(v = \nu\lambda\) must hold in both media with the same \(\nu\).

**The relation.** Dividing the two forms of \(v = \nu\lambda\):

\(\mu = \dfrac{c}{v} = \dfrac{\nu\lambda_{\text{air}}}{\nu\lambda_{\text{medium}}} = \dfrac{\lambda_{\text{air}}}{\lambda_{\text{medium}}}\)

so the refractive index is simply the **ratio of the wavelengths**.

\(\mu = \dfrac{600}{400}\)

\(\mu = 1{\cdot}5\)

**The direction of the change is the check.** The wavelength has **shortened**, from 600 nm to 400 nm, so the medium is optically denser than air and \(\mu\) must come out greater than 1. Inverting the ratio would give \(0{\cdot}667\), which is not offered — and rightly, since no ordinary medium has a refractive index below 1.

**A common misreading worth naming.** It is tempting to think the light has "turned blue" on entering the medium, since 400 nm is blue in air. It has not. **Colour is a matter of frequency**, and the frequency here is unchanged at \(5 \times 10^{14}\) Hz throughout. A diver sees no colour shift underwater for exactly this reason. The light is still the same orange-red light; only its wavelength inside the glass is shorter, and it returns to 600 nm the moment it emerges.

rows.stem: In a Young's double slit experiment, the separation between the two slits is d and distance of the screen from the slits is 1000 d. If the first minima falls at a distance d from the central maximum, obtain the relation between d and \(\lambda\).
rows.solution:
**Setting it up.** In Young's experiment a **dark** fringe falls where the path difference from the two slits is an odd multiple of half a wavelength. For a point at distance \(x\) from the centre on a screen \(D\) away, the path difference is \(xd/D\), so the \(n\)th minimum sits at

\(\dfrac{x_n d}{D} = (2n - 1)\dfrac{\lambda}{2} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x_n = \dfrac{(2n - 1)\lambda D}{2d}\)

**For the FIRST minimum**, \(n = 1\), and the bracket is just 1:

\(x_1 = \dfrac{\lambda D}{2d}\)

This is the step the question turns on. The first dark fringe corresponds to a path difference of \(\lambda/2\) — a **half**, not three halves.

**Substituting the given geometry.** With \(D = 1000d\):

\(x_1 = \dfrac{\lambda \times 1000d}{2d} = 500\lambda\)

and the stem states that this first minimum falls at a distance \(d\) from the central maximum, so \(x_1 = d\):

\(d = 500\lambda \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \lambda = \dfrac{d}{500}\)

**The published scheme gives \(d = 1500\lambda\), and that is an error.** It writes the position of the first minimum as \(x_1 = \dfrac{3}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\lambda D}{d}\), which is \(\dfrac{3\lambda D}{2d}\) — the formula for the **second** minimum, where the path difference is \(3\lambda/2\). Putting \(n = 1\) into \((2n-1)\lambda D/2d\) gives \(\lambda D/2d\), a factor of three smaller, and hence \(d = 500\lambda\).

**A check that settles it without any formula.** The path difference at the first dark fringe is \(\lambda/2\) by definition, and the path difference at a point \(x\) from the centre is \(xd/D\). Setting \(xd/D = \lambda/2\) with \(x = d\) and \(D = 1000d\):

\(\dfrac{d \cdot d}{1000d} = \dfrac{\lambda}{2} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dfrac{d}{1000} = \dfrac{\lambda}{2} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad d = 500\lambda\)

**What the answer means.** The slit separation is 500 wavelengths — for green light of 500 nm, a quarter of a millimetre, which is exactly the order of magnitude a real double-slit apparatus uses.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem: A point object in air is placed symmetrically at a distance of 60 cm in front of a concave spherical surface of refractive index 1.5. If the radius of curvature of the surface is 20 cm, find the position of the image formed.
rows.solution:
**Refraction at a single spherical surface**, with light going from medium 1 into medium 2:

\(\dfrac{n_2}{v} - \dfrac{n_1}{u} = \dfrac{n_2 - n_1}{R}\)

**Fixing the signs**, all distances measured from the surface with the incident light travelling in the positive direction:

- \(n_1 = 1\) (air), \(n_2 = 1{\cdot}5\) (the glass)
- \(u = -60\ \mathrm{cm}\) — the object is on the incoming side
- \(R = -20\ \mathrm{cm}\) — the surface is **concave** towards the object, so its centre of curvature lies on the same side as the object

That sign on \(R\) is the whole of the question. A concave surface facing the object has a negative radius; take it as \(+20\) and the answer changes sign and size together.

**Substituting.**

\(\dfrac{1{\cdot}5}{v} - \dfrac{1}{-60} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}5 - 1}{-20}\)

\(\dfrac{1{\cdot}5}{v} + \dfrac{1}{60} = -\dfrac{0{\cdot}5}{20} = -0{\cdot}025\)

\(\dfrac{1{\cdot}5}{v} = -0{\cdot}025 - 0{\cdot}0167 = -0{\cdot}0417\)

\(v = -36\ \mathrm{cm}\)

**The image is virtual, formed 36 cm from the surface on the same side as the object** — that is, in the air, in front of the glass, not inside it.

**Why virtual was inevitable.** A concave refracting surface with the denser medium behind it is **diverging** for light entering from the rarer side: both the shape of the surface and the change of medium bend the rays outwards. Diverging rays cannot meet, so no real image can form, whatever the object distance. The negative \(v\) is therefore a result to expect rather than one to double-check.

Note also that the image lies **closer** to the surface than the object (36 cm against 60 cm), which is the usual behaviour of a diverging element.

rows.stem:
A series RL circuit with R = 10 \(\Omega\) and L = \(\left(\dfrac{100}{\pi}\right)\) mH is connected to an ac source of voltage V = 141 sin (100 \(\pi\) t), where V is in volts and t is in seconds. Calculate
(a) impedence of the circuit
(b) phase angle, and
(c) voltage drop across the inductor
rows.solution:
**Reading the source.** \(V = 141\sin(100\pi t)\), so \(V_0 = 141\) V and \(\omega = 100\pi\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\) (that is, \(f = 50\) Hz). The rms voltage is

\(V_{rms} = \dfrac{141}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 100\ \mathrm{V}\)

— the numbers are chosen so that 141 is \(100\sqrt{2}\).

**(a) The impedance.**

The inductive reactance comes first, and the \(\pi\) cancels by design:

\(X_L = \omega L = 100\pi \times \dfrac{100}{\pi} \times 10^{-3} = 100 \times 100 \times 10^{-3} = 10\ \Omega\)

Resistance and reactance combine **in quadrature**, not by simple addition, because the voltage across \(R\) is in phase with the current while the voltage across \(L\) leads it by \(90^\circ\):

\(Z = \sqrt{R^{2} + X_L^{2}} = \sqrt{10^{2} + 10^{2}} = \sqrt{200}\)

\(Z = 10\sqrt{2} \approx 14{\cdot}1\ \Omega\)

Adding them arithmetically would give \(20\ \Omega\), and that is the error the question is set to expose.

**(b) The phase angle.**

\(\tan\phi = \dfrac{X_L}{R} = \dfrac{10}{10} = 1\)

\(\phi = \dfrac{\pi}{4} = 45^\circ\)

The **current lags the voltage** by \(45^\circ\), as it must in any circuit whose reactance is inductive.

**(c) The voltage drop across the inductor.**

\(I_{rms} = \dfrac{V_{rms}}{Z} = \dfrac{141/\sqrt{2}}{10\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{141}{20} = 7{\cdot}05\ \mathrm{A}\)

\(V_L = I_{rms}X_L = 7{\cdot}05 \times 10\)

\(V_L = 70{\cdot}5\ \mathrm{V}\)

**The check that makes the quadrature rule vivid.** The drop across the resistor is \(V_R = I_{rms}R = 70{\cdot}5\) V as well, so the two drops sum to 141 V — while the source supplies only 100 V rms. There is no contradiction: the two voltages are \(90^\circ\) out of phase and must be added as vectors,

\(\sqrt{V_R^{2} + V_L^{2}} = \sqrt{70{\cdot}5^{2} + 70{\cdot}5^{2}} = 70{\cdot}5\sqrt{2} \approx 100\ \mathrm{V}\)

which is exactly the source voltage. In an ac circuit the individual voltage drops can each exceed the supply; only their **phasor** sum is constrained.

rows.stem: A ray of light is incident on a glass prism of refractive index \(\mu\) and refracting angle A. If it just suffers total internal reflection at the other face, obtain a relation between the angle of incidence, angle of prism and critical angle.
rows.solution:
**The situation.** A ray enters face AB at angle of incidence \(i\), refracts to \(r_1\) inside the glass, crosses to the second face AC and meets it at \(r_2\). The phrase "**just** suffers total internal reflection" is the key datum: it means \(r_2\) is exactly at the threshold, neither less (where the ray would emerge) nor more (where it would already be reflected).

\(r_2 = i_c\)

**The prism relation.** For any prism the two internal angles sum to the refracting angle:

\(A = r_1 + r_2\)

That itself follows from the geometry of the quadrilateral formed by the two normals and the two faces: the normals meet at \(180^\circ - A\), and the angles of the triangle they make with the ray give \(r_1 + r_2 = A\).

Substituting the threshold condition:

\(A = r_1 + i_c \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad r_1 = A - i_c\)

**Snell's law at the first face**, where the ray enters from air:

\(\sin i = \mu\sin r_1\)

and putting in \(r_1\):

\(\boxed{\ \sin i = \mu\sin(A - i_c)\ }\)

which is the relation asked for. It may also be written entirely in terms of \(i_c\), since \(\mu = \dfrac{1}{\sin i_c}\):

\(\sin i = \dfrac{\sin(A - i_c)}{\sin i_c}\)

**How to read the result.** For a given prism, this fixes the **smallest** angle of incidence at which light can still get out of the second face. Make \(i\) any smaller and \(r_1\) shrinks, so \(r_2 = A - r_1\) grows past \(i_c\), the ray is totally internally reflected at AC, and nothing emerges there at all.

**Two limiting cases worth checking.** If \(A = 2i_c\) then \(r_1 = i_c\) and \(\sin i = \mu\sin i_c = 1\), so \(i = 90^\circ\): the ray must grazing-incidence the first face, and any prism with \(A > 2i_c\) lets no light through its second face whatever the angle of entry. And if \(A = i_c\) then \(r_1 = 0\), so \(i = 0\) — the ray enters along the normal.

For an equilateral crown-glass prism \((A = 60^\circ,\ \mu = 1{\cdot}5,\ i_c = 41{\cdot}8^\circ)\) the formula gives \(\sin i = 1{\cdot}5\sin 18{\cdot}2^\circ = 0{\cdot}468\), so \(i \approx 27{\cdot}9^\circ\) — the minimum incidence for an emergent ray.

rows.stem: Two cells of emf \(\mathrm{E}_1\) and \(\mathrm{E}_2\) and internal resistances \(r_1\) and \(r_2\) are connected in parallel, with their terminals of the same polarity connected together. Obtain an expression for the equivalent emf of the combination.
rows.solution:
**The arrangement.** Two cells are connected in parallel between the same two points \(B_1\) and \(B_2\), with like terminals joined, so both drive current the same way. Let \(V = V(B_1) - V(B_2)\) be the common terminal potential difference, and let the cells deliver currents \(I_1\) and \(I_2\) into the external circuit, which draws \(I\).

**Two facts do all the work:** the cells share the same \(V\) because they are joined at both ends, and their currents add because charge is conserved at the junction.

**The terminal voltage of each cell.**

\(V = E_1 - I_1r_1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad I_1 = \dfrac{E_1 - V}{r_1}\)

\(V = E_2 - I_2r_2 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad I_2 = \dfrac{E_2 - V}{r_2}\)

**Adding the currents.**

\(I = I_1 + I_2 = \dfrac{E_1 - V}{r_1} + \dfrac{E_2 - V}{r_2}\)

\(I = \left(\dfrac{E_1}{r_1} + \dfrac{E_2}{r_2}\right) - V\left(\dfrac{1}{r_1} + \dfrac{1}{r_2}\right)\)

**Rearranging for \(V\).**

\(V\left(\dfrac{r_1 + r_2}{r_1r_2}\right) = \dfrac{E_1r_2 + E_2r_1}{r_1r_2} - I\)

\(V = \dfrac{E_1r_2 + E_2r_1}{r_1 + r_2} - I\left(\dfrac{r_1r_2}{r_1 + r_2}\right)\)

**Identifying the equivalent cell.** This has exactly the form \(V = E_{eq} - Ir_{eq}\), which is the terminal-voltage equation of a *single* cell. Comparing term by term:

\(E_{eq} = \dfrac{E_1r_2 + E_2r_1}{r_1 + r_2} \qquad\text{and}\qquad r_{eq} = \dfrac{r_1r_2}{r_1 + r_2}\)

**Reading the result.** Note the **cross-multiplication**: each emf is weighted by the *other* cell's internal resistance. That is not a slip but the physics — the cell with the *smaller* internal resistance has the larger say, because it can drive current more freely. Writing \((E_1r_1 + E_2r_2)/(r_1+r_2)\) is the standard error and weights them exactly backwards.

The equivalent internal resistance is the ordinary parallel combination, and it is **smaller than either** \(r_1\) or \(r_2\) — which is the point of connecting cells in parallel: to supply a larger current than one cell could manage alone.

**Two special cases as checks.** If the cells are identical \((E_1 = E_2 = E,\ r_1 = r_2 = r)\) then \(E_{eq} = E\) and \(r_{eq} = r/2\): the same emf, half the internal resistance, exactly as expected. And if \(r_1 \ll r_2\), then \(E_{eq} \to E_1\) — the stronger-driving cell dominates completely.
